claims.text: Elemental Cr coatings on zirconium-alloy cladding are prone to premature failure through elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
The proposed intervention is to replace pure Cr with a Cr–Al coating containing approximately 5 at.% Al.
Cr–Al is a relevant metallic coating class for improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance of zirconium-alloy cladding.
Adding approximately 5 at.% Al to Cr will inhibit high-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
The Al addition will produce an adherent, continuous Al2O3 layer along the coating interface.
Al in the Cr–Al coating will preferentially oxidize under high-temperature conditions.
Preferential oxidation of Al will form a stable alumina scale.
The alumina layer will act as a slow-diffusing barrier to Cr and Zr.
Slower Cr–Zr interdiffusion will reduce coating degradation and preserve coating integrity.
Relative to pure Cr, the Cr–Al coating will exhibit less Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Relative to pure Cr, the Cr–Al coating will have improved structural integrity after high-temperature steam exposure.
The Cr–Al coating will sustain oxidation protection during accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposure.
The Cr–Al coating will maintain excellent corrosion protection during normal subcritical-water operation.
Normal-operation conditions are represented by subcritical or simulated PWR primary water at approximately 300°C.
Accident-relevant conditions are represented by high-temperature steam transients up to approximately 850–900°C.
Normal-water service involves extended exposure, whereas the 850–900°C steam exposure is short-term.
The optimal Al concentration and the effective upper-temperature boundary remain uncertain.
Failure to obtain reduced Cr–Zr interdiffusion and a continuous alumina layer, or failure to outperform pure Cr in overall oxidation or corrosion, would falsify the hypothesis.
